opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, because I think there's been a bit of a narrative shift. When the GCG paper came out, the optimized adversarial suffixes, those strings of what looks like random tokens, that was a real wake-up call. It showed you could automatically search for inputs that reliably break a model's safety training, and that some of those attacks even transferred across models.

Since then, frontier labs have gotten a lot better at defending against that specific class of attack. Perplexity filters catch a lot of it, because gibberish strings look very unlike natural text. Adversarial training on these kinds of suffixes helps too. Input and output classifiers help as well. So if you take an off-the-shelf GCG suffix and paste it into a frontier model today, it's probably not going to work very well.

But I'd caution against concluding that the underlying problem has gone away. A few points.

First, the defenses are often fairly narrow. You can patch the particular attack distribution you trained on, but attackers adapt. You can add a fluency constraint to the optimization and get attacks that read as natural language and slip past perplexity filters. Or you can use another model to generate the attacks, iterating on persuasive or obfuscated prompts. The surface form changes, but the vulnerability is still there.

Second, gibberish attacks remain very useful as a research tool, especially for open-weight models where you have gradient access. They're a kind of worst-case probe. If a model can be broken by optimization in a few minutes of compute, that tells you the safety training is fairly shallow, even if casual users would never find that input. That's the lesson from our work on superhuman Go AIs: systems that look extremely capable in normal use can have glaring holes that an adversary can find with search. Robustness doesn't come for free with capability.

Third, the threat model matters. For closed models behind an API, a lot of the action has moved to other attack surfaces: many-shot jailbreaking, multi-turn attacks, fine-tuning APIs where small amounts of harmful data can strip out safeguards, and, increasingly, prompt injection in agentic settings. That last one worries me more over time, because the attacker doesn't even need to be the user. They just need to put text somewhere the agent will read it.

So my summary is that gibberish strings as a practical attack on hardened frontier systems are less potent than two years ago, but as evidence about how robust these models fundamentally are, they're still telling us something important. We haven't solved adversarial robustness. We've raised the cost of some specific attacks, which is valuable, but the cat-and-mouse dynamic is very much ongoing. As models become more capable and get deployed with more autonomy, the stakes of losing that game go up.

r001.rationale: It says attackers can adapt by adding fluency constraints or iteratively generating persuasive or obfuscated attacks, changing the surface form while preserving the vulnerability.

r002.rationale: It mentions past transfer across models and stronger frontier defenses, but not increasingly divergent proprietary-model training pipelines reducing white-box jailbreak transfer.

r003.rationale: It mentions persuasive and obfuscated prompts, but does not explain adaptive optimization strengthening a social-engineering jailbreak that already partially bypasses safeguards.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the gibberish-string attacks, the GCG-style adversarial suffixes, are interesting because they occupy a weird middle ground. On one hand they've become less practically useful as a day-to-day jailbreak, and on the other hand they remain really important as a scientific tool.

On the practical side, the frontier labs have gotten better at defending against them. Part of that is just that the strings are so weird looking. A random sequence of tokens with exclamation marks and fragments of code is easy to flag with a perplexity filter or a classifier, because no human ever types that way. So if you're a company trying to stop this, you have a very clean signal to work with. The attacks also often don't transfer as well as people hoped. You optimize against an open-weight model, you get something that works there, and then you try it on a closed model and maybe it works some fraction of the time, maybe not at all after the next update. And because they're optimized token sequences, they tend to be brittle. Small changes to the system prompt or a bit of input sanitization can break them.

But I'd push back on anyone who concludes they don't matter anymore. The reason I still care about them is that they tell you something about the underlying robustness of the model, as opposed to the robustness of the whole deployed system. If the model still has a mode where a sequence of nonsense tokens flips it into complying with something harmful, then you haven't actually fixed the model. You've put a filter in front of it. And filters are the kind of thing that fail in new deployment contexts. If the model is reading tool outputs, or web pages, or documents from untrusted sources, suddenly weird strings showing up in the context is totally normal, and a perplexity filter on user input doesn't help you at all. Agentic settings are exactly where you'd expect this class of attack to come back.

The other thing is that the optimization-based approach keeps evolving. The pure gibberish version was the first thing that worked, but you can constrain the search to produce fluent text, or combine gradient-based search with LLM-driven rewriting, and now you've got something that looks like a plausible paragraph and is much harder to filter. So I think of the random-string attacks less as a specific threat and more as the simplest instance of a broader fact, which is that we can automatically search for inputs that break these models, and the models aren't robust to that search. The specific artifacts get patched, but the capability to generate them hasn't gone away.

So my overall assessment is: as a jailbreak someone would use in the wild, their heyday is probably behind us for the major chat products. As a measure of whether we've solved adversarial robustness, they're still telling us the answer is no.

r001.rationale: The response links the attacks’ continuing significance to evolving optimization methods, including fluent-text constraints and LLM-driven rewriting.

r002.rationale: It says open-weight attacks may transfer inconsistently to closed models, but does not attribute this to increasingly divergent proprietary-model training pipelines.

r003.rationale: It describes making optimized attacks more fluent and harder to filter, but does not discuss strengthening a social-engineering jailbreak that already partly bypasses safeguards.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re still useful as a way of testing how robust these systems actually are. A string can look like gibberish to a human and still reliably change a model’s behavior. If your safety mechanism breaks under that kind of input, that’s a real limitation, even if it’s not how a typical user would interact with the system.

But I’d distinguish finding a jailbreak from demonstrating a practical attack. Does it work across different requests? Does it transfer to another model, or survive a model update? How much access and computation did you need to find it? A successful attack against one particular checkpoint is evidence of a vulnerability, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you how easy that vulnerability is to exploit in deployment.

So I wouldn’t dismiss them because they look unnatural. I also wouldn’t treat the success rate of one particular method as a complete measure of safety. We want defenses that hold up when the attacker changes their approach, rather than defenses that just block the strings we’ve already found.

r001.rationale: The response says attackers may change their approach, but does not connect gibberish-jailbreak effectiveness to adaptive optimization.

r002.rationale: It asks whether an attack transfers to another model, but does not suggest that diverging proprietary training pipelines reduce white-box jailbreak transfer.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss social-engineering jailbreaks or how adaptive optimization could strengthen one that already partly bypasses safeguards.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re still useful, particularly as a way of probing how robust the underlying defenses actually are. A string can look like gibberish to us and still reliably cause a model to behave differently. The fact that a human wouldn’t naturally write it doesn’t make that failure irrelevant, especially when an attacker can automate the search.

But I’d distinguish that from how useful a particular string is in practice. Does it work only on the model you optimized it against, or does it transfer? Does it survive an update? Can you find it with the access and compute an attacker would realistically have? Those questions matter much more than whether the string looks meaningful.

So I wouldn’t dismiss them, but I also wouldn’t treat success on one set of gibberish attacks as evidence that you’ve solved jailbreaks. You need to evaluate against attackers who can adapt to the defense.

r001.rationale: The response says attackers can automate the search and emphasizes evaluating against attackers who adapt to the defense, linking continued usefulness to adaptive optimization.

r002.rationale: It discusses transfer and model updates generally, but does not suggest that increasingly divergent proprietary-model training pipelines reduce white-box jailbreak transfer.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss social-engineering jailbreaks or explain how adaptive optimization could strengthen one that already partially bypasses safeguards.
